utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Captain Drljan. Can I remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Drljan, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We'll resume our examination-in-chief where we left off last Friday. My last question to you was: Where were you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, I was at the forward command post. That's in the early morning of the 6th. Later, I left for Zarkovica, where there was the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what you did on that morning, the morning of the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I woke up, before I started working, I came to the operational centre of the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was there anything going on at the forward command post, more specifically, in the operational centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice anything particular, anything out of the ordinary, except that frigate Captain Kozaric was making some entries in the military -- in the war logbook. At that time, the phone rang. I answered the phone. It was usual for anyone who was closest to the phone to pick up the receiver and to take any notes that needed to be taken, anything to be written down. I answered the phone, and warship Captain Zec ordered me to go to Zarkovica to see Captain First Class Vladimir Kovacevic and to convey orders from the commander, Admiral Jokic, he must not fire on the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At what time did the call come in? I know it's been a long time, but please tell us, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was between 10 past 7.00 and a quarter past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please make a short pause between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you. What did you do after you received that call?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having received that call, I went back to my room to put on some warm clothes. There was a strong wind on that day and it was quite cold. As soon as I got dressed, I went downstairs. I had breakfast in a hurry and I went outside to find a driver and a car that could take me to Zarkovica, where I had been ordered to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So did you in fact leave for Zarkovica that morning?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I apologise for starting my answer immediately, to the interpreters. I left for Zarkovica immediately and I reached Zarkovica at about 8.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Once at Zarkovica, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I got there, I got out of the car. I had left the car right there at the beginning, because I saw that there was firing. And I went into the bunker, which is where Captain First Class Kovacevic was, and he exercised command from there. He was wearing a headset that was connected to the phone lines, and he was giving orders to his units. I entered and I conveyed to him the orders that had been issued by Jokic, and I wanted to make sure whether he had understood the orders. He nodded, which for me was a sign that he had understood the orders. So I left the bunker, in order to not be in the way of him exercising command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain exactly how he nodded. The way he nodded, was it clear to you that he had understood what you had conveyed to him, the message?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond a shadow of a doubt. Because what I had told him was, "Captain, Commander Jokic has ordered you not to fire on the Old Town." He was looking straight at me as I was saying these words. He knew that I was an officer from the command. And each and every subordinate officer pays close attention whenever an officer from the command walks into their room. So he was looking at me all the time and he was nodding to let me know that he had understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You told us that you didn't want to be in the way while he was giving orders to his troops. So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left and I headed for a low-squat wall that was at the end of a clearing, that is, just above the Old Town. Because it was from that point that you had the best visibility in terms of being able to observe what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So having arrived at Zarkovica and, as you said, you realised that Captain Kovacevic was giving orders, was in the process of giving orders, from that place, could you actually see what was going on around you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wind, the bora wind was very strong on that day and the weather was clear. Visibility was excellent and I could actually see as far as the Old Town. Everything was perfectly clear, and I could also see Srdj, which was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for about one hour, so I left Zarkovica at about 9.00. And I left for the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you went back to Kupari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the time you spent at Zarkovica during that one hour, did you observe Srdj and the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I observed both Srdj and the Old Town. I was interested. I wanted to see what was going on, like everyone else was. Captain Kovacevic's units had begun to move towards Srdj, because their objective was to take Srdj. They reached a small elevation just before Srdj and they stopped right there. That's what I saw happening on Srdj at that point in time. I also saw shells falling around Srdj, so shells fired from artillery pieces exploding just at the foot of Srdj and behind Srdj, those that had flown over Srdj. I can't exactly tell you how many shells. I didn't count them in or out, but I saw shells exploding. As for the old part of town --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Excuse me my interruption, please, but could you tell me the following: Those shells that were falling on Srdj as you were watching, could you tell where those shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those shells, it's very difficult to follow the trajectory of a shell. You don't actually see it. Those were shells from artillery pieces with a programmed trajectory. So they were falling down vertically. At that point in time, I was in no position to tell where the shells were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: Did you watch Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I watched Dubrovnik's Old Town, which is what you can see very clearly from Zarkovica. I saw several fires inside the Old Town. One of these fires was on the Stradun. Stradun roughly splits the Old Town down the middle, the northern section and the southern section. Closer to us there was black smoke, pitch-black smoke coming out of a building in the section of town closer to us. I took my binoculars to see whether the roof of that house had been damaged, and I saw that the roof had not been damaged. So I couldn't make heads nor tails of it, why the smoke was coming out. You couldn't see the windows, but smoke was coming out towards the Stradun, black smoke coming out. And then I saw another fire further down. There was a building that was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was there anything else you observed in the Old Town in addition to these fires and the smoke that you have described?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 or 20 minutes later, midway down the Stradun, a huge gate had been opened and a man walked out with another man who was helping him. A big man, about your height, but bulkier, burlier. They pushed a mortar out onto the Stradun and they opened fire, firing only a single shell, or at least I saw them fire only a single shell, after which --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did they do after they had fired that shell?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After firing that shell, they lingered on for about a minute, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I place an objection, Your Honour? The 65 ter summary that we have received does not indicate that this witness has seen a mortar fire from the Old Town. What is indicated here is that the witness saw a mortar in the Old Town. That's all. And this testimony is going beyond the 65 ter summary that has been supplied to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've submitted our proofing notes to our learned friends and colleagues on two occasions, because the proofing itself was done a bit later, so there were certain inaccuracies in the first part; and in the second part of our proofing notes, we specified the positions inside the Old Town, the ones that this witness observed, and we sent this on Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you notified that there was firing?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think it would be all right for me to testify on behalf of this witness in relation to the Old Town. Because what we have said so far is not all the information concerning what he observed in the Old Town. There is talk of firing inside the Old Town too. However, as I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The note that was sent to the OTP, as for this specific position, this specific mortar that the witness has just referred to, the OTP has been notified. I can't remember whether it was proofing notes, the part about opening fire, but I do know that we informed them about that mortar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point of the objection is that there was no notification of firing, and from what you're saying, that appears to be the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all likelihood, Your Honour, but I believe my colleague has the proofing notes, and that's exactly what we informed them about. I know about the mortar for sure. I'm not sure if we put anything about the actual firing from that mortar there. I don't have the notes with me now, but if my learned friend and colleague could just go through them, I'm sure she'll see that this is exactly what we are talking about and what we informed the OTP about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is precisely the point that she is making, that she has them and there is no mention of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That must be so, Your Honour, because we did write that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise you run the danger of having evidence excluded, evidence that you may think is particularly material?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do realise that, Your Honour. Maybe then I should accept that I have made a mistake, because it was down to me to inform my colleagues from the OTP about that particular proofing session. There may have been an error, after all, because I did go through the corrected proofing notes, revised proofing notes, and I included a very important bit of information in relation to something that the OTP wants to know about, something that was not included in the first proofing notes, something in relation to this witness's testimony, and that was operations against the Old Town, specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber proposes to admit the evidence on this occasion, Mr. Rodic, despite the objection, noting that there was at least expressed notification about the weapon itself, though not the firing. But this has become increasingly a problem, and we must put you on notice that we are going to take a more positive and direct view about it for the future. So I would suggest that you take particular care from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Can I please have the usher's assistance now. I would like to show the witness the map that was marked P10.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we please put the map there where we can see the position of the Old Town, as centrally as possible. Mr. Drljan, can you please help by positioning this map in the centre so that we can see this part to the right of the town. Can you point on this map the position that you were at. Take the pointer, please, and show the position on the map. Not on the monitor; on the map, Mr. Drljan.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanka Zarkovica. This is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us where Zarkovica is on this map. Where is it written "Zarkovica"? Can you please take a look.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north-east of Dubrovnik, but I don't see the name Zarkovica. At least, I can't find it. Here is Strincjera, Srdj, Bosanka, so Zarkovica should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we please take the next map, P11.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where Zarkovica is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And that was the vantage point that you observed the Old Town from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we please have map P11 placed before the witness. I apologise. It's my mistake. We need actually the map P13. P13. I apologise once again to the usher and to the Honourable Chamber. Could you please push it upwards a little bit. That's right. Mr. Drljan, do you recognise what this map shows?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the position that you had just described, first the houses that you saw. Could you indicate them on the map.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately this house. I cannot say 100 per cent that I'm sure whether this one or this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What are you pointing particularly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house where this black smoke was spewing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where did you see the mortar that you had just described?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately somewhere in the middle of the Stradun street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn the map in relation to the position of Zarkovica from where you were observing the town. So put the map in that position, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I was looking in this direction, and the mortar was brought out from this building, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which part of the Old Town do you see viewing from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the whole town from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where is the harbour?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to the left, viewing from Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you now indicate on the map the buildings that you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building here, where this black mark is, I saw this black smoke coming out of this building, and it went first toward the Stradun and then lifted up above the roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you hold on, please, a second. The building that you are showing now is the map that has this black suitcase form on it. Where was the other building that you saw on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number, please, if you can be more specific, or the name of the street, if you can read it.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the streets of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we indicate precisely on the map this location so that we can have better orientation.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is from Od Puca, in this circle, one of the buildings was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that was the second building that you saw on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the smoke was lighter, kind of bluish, and I saw flames as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you saw anything else in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, after this mortar fired one shell, and after it had been pulled into the gate --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you show us the position of this mortar now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second one that I saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You spoke about one mortar.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately here, halfway down the Stradun street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. This material is not in the 65 ter information given at all. There is no reference to another mortar. There is only reference to one mortar being seen by this witness. And this is completely additional information which goes beyond 65 ter material.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness corrected himself. I just wanted him to show the position of this -- the one mortar that he had mentioned. He made a mistake. There was no second mortar, nor was there any mention of its position. So I wanted him to indicate the mortar that he had seen on the Stradun and that he had testified to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So can you please show us the position where you saw the mortar that you had mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right of this black rectangle there's a row of buildings there, and the mortar was pulled out from a large gate to the Stradun street. It fired one shell and it was pulled back into the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that is slightly to the right from this black rectangle, and across is the street Izmedju Polaca; is that right? It runs parallel with the Stradun street.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Behind that building is the Iza Polaca [as interpreted] street. That is what I see now on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, tell us, did you see anything else in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I saw flares behind the Orlando column.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you show that on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- behind this column, I saw flares, which means that fire had been opened from some kind of firing piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see the weapon itself?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because it was hidden behind the Orlando column. But I did see the flares as a result of a shell firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you have indicated the position behind the Orlando column?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, did you see anything else in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a couple of our shells landing very close to the place where this mortar had been pulled out earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You saw the mortars landing, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where did it land? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Stradun street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please show us the approximate position of the landing.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the street itself. It's very close to the building from which the mortar had been pulled out and then pulled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it is also the position to the right from the black rectangle and opposite it is the Od Puca street which runs parallel with the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that all that you saw in the Old Town on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is all. I also saw another flame -- smoke, but I don't know what was the source of the smoke. It was coming approximately from the area where the harbour was, but please understand, I cannot focus exactly on the position when there was a very strong wind and I couldn't see the source of fire. The wind was dispersing the smoke and I couldn't locate the position exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you described flares that you had seen near the Orlando column, you said that that was the fire flares from a weapon being fired from. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a military person. I know how, for instance, a mortar fires, and that was a flare from a mortar, which appears before the barrel of the weapon, and this flare is up to one metre long. But also I could deduce that it was a mortar also according to other elements. It couldn't have been a gun, which has a straight trajectory, whereas mortar has a curved trajectory. So if they wanted to target our forces, they could only do that with a mortar or with a Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that is all that you saw on that day from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because soon thereafter I left that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please just take your time in answering my questions. You said that you spent about an hour on that point.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Kupari. Since I didn't have a proper breakfast, I had something to eat. And then I went to the operations centre, where I stayed until the time when I left again for Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were at Zarkovica that one hour that you spent there, you mentioned Captain Kovacevic. Did you see any of the senior officers at Zarkovica? Were there any of them there at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the bunker, from where Kovacevic was commanding, I only saw his communications personnel and a couple of other men whom I didn't recognise because I didn't know them. The only one that I recognised among them was Kovacevic, and no one else. Outside the bunker were a few people whom I also hadn't known before. There were lots of reservists and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Kupari, you said you went to the operations centre, until you left again for Zarkovica. When was that, approximately, when you left again for Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Zarkovica again slightly before 1400 hours. I think I arrived there at 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kupari, did you spend the whole time at the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please show the witness the Exhibit D96. Mr. Drljan, on page 67 of this log, or diary, we have entries relating to the 6th December 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise who made these entries here on this page?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me who it was that made these entries.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one at 0500 hours was made by Sikimic, Vlado Sikimic, and at 5.30 again it is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How come you know he did it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recognise his handwriting, and also here are his initials, VS.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps who made the following entries?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6.50, 7.05, 7.15, 7.30. All those entries were made by frigate Captain Kozaric. Like 7.45 too, except that he didn't sign his name. 7.40, 7.45, and 7.47, that is, on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it's Kozaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five entries were signed. Two he did not sign, but it's the same handwriting and I can recognise his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you make any entries in this diary; and if so, could you please tell me which ones are yours. On page 68, did you write anything there? Are there any entries of yours there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. On page 68, there are no entries that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about page 69?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 69, there is the entry of 12.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So did you make that entry at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When returning from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, and I made this entry. It can be seen that Kozaric made most of the entries; however, at that moment he was busy with something, so I made this entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: So you received this message from the European Mission, addressed to the command of the Military Naval Sector Boka at 12.25; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this. This message has about three paragraphs. Please look at the last sentence in the first paragraph. It says: "At the same time, we denounce any provocative actions from Srdj and Lapad which would be a pretext for violating the cease-fire," if I read this out properly. The next sentence: "We state with full responsibility that allegations of our force's actions have been construed so as to provide an excuse for the attempt to conquer Srdj." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about from the forward command post? Was any message sent from VPS Boka to Dubrovnik with such contents, stating that the Croatian forces were shooting from Srdj and Lapad?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, no such message was sent. I came even earlier. And also, it is not written in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If such a message did exist, could it have been sent from some other place?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been sent from the basic command post through Radio Bar or through the command of Mokosica, where we had direct communications with the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: On page 69, is that the only entry that you made?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 69, that's the only entry that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are there any entries made by you on page 70?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some entries that I made on that page, that is, at 1305.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since there are two entries made at 1305, can you read us the one that you made.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The order of the commander of the 9th VPS to Captain Kovacevic was transmitted not to fire on the town but to act only in the immediate vicinity of Srdj." Captain warship Zec [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what this is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warship Captain Zec ordered that Kovacevic should be warned again not to fire, only to fire at Srdj, and that's why it says in the remark: "Warship Captain Zec." That is to say, that he was the source of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: You said that about 2.00 in the afternoon, about 1400 hours, you went to Zarkovica again.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did you do there? Did you get to Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did get to Zarkovica, to see how the situation was developing further. I glanced at the old part of Dubrovnik and I saw smoke coming from several different places. However, I was more interested in Srdj, because I saw that Kovacevic was getting ready to withdraw forces from Srdj, which I heard in passing, because I passed by and stopped at his bunker. He was issuing orders for tanks to be prepared in order to get to Srdj, right below Srdj, and to protect this large number of tanks and, under their protection, to withdraw a large number of troops so that they would not be hurt or injured during the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At that time, was there any firing at Srdj?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, still, but the shells were few and far between. The intensity was not like it was before. Every now and then a shell would fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: In addition to Kovacevic, were there any other officers at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any other officers from the command, because they are the only ones that I know. It was the same people who I saw there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you stay any longer at Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there until before dusk; that is to say, the sun was still up. I saw the withdrawal of Kovacevic's forces from Srdj, the protection -- under the protection of the tanks, and when he withdrew his very last soldier, I decided, because I knew that there had been casualties, I had heard about that, I decided to go to Bosanka where one of his companies was to talk to these people a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you actually go to Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go to Bosanka. I entered the building where most of his soldiers were - from his company, that is - and I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the soldiers who had been at Srdj?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the soldiers. All of them had been on Srdj at that day, that is to say, with a view to taking Srdj. I talked to them, and I talked to one officer. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the soldiers tell you something, or did you tell them something?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came there. I greeted them. But they first said that I was the only officer from the command who came there to see them. And they started complaining to me, and they were telling me, angrily, that they needed 130-millimetre artillery, 130-millimetre guns, that they were supposed to get such support and they did not get it. In their words, Jokic did not give this support, although it had been agreed upon, allegedly on the previous day. So they were very angry on account of that, because they thought that if they had had this support, they would not have lost their comrades who were killed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Bosanka? Until when?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed at Bosanka until dusk. So sometime after 1600 hours. After 1600 hours, I set out from Bosanka back to Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you return to the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: On that day - that is to say, the last page we looked at was page 72 of the log - did you make any other entries into the war logbook on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is precisely on page 72. When I returned from Srdj, I did not put the time. This happened sometime between 1630 and 1810. This is a radiogram, or rather, a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: What is the message that you entered?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: When does it come? After which message?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1627.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it what it says here, "Crisis Staff Dubrovnik for KVPS Boka"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Are there any other entries by the end of that day, until the end of that day? Could you please look at the logbook further on. That is to say, until the end of the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking now. No. No. There were no other entries of mine after this one about the Crisis Staff sending a telegram to the VPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: While you were at the operations centre on that day - the time that you spent there, that is - did you perhaps have any contacts with the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- I'm sorry. I'm going to withdraw this question. In the morning, around 10 past or 15 past 7.00, you said that Zec called you and he issued you an order to go to Zarkovica to convey a message to Kovacevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: An order to Kovacevic. And at 1305, you also made an entry to the effect that an order should be conveyed to Captain Kovacevic not to fire at the town itself but only at Srdj, and this was ordered to you by --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: -- warship Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please just wait for me to finish my question and then start answering.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order that I entered there was actually made by warship Captain Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in both cases, did you contact Captain Zec by telephone?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, did you see warship Captain Zec at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: At any point in time, did anybody from the command of the military naval sector ask you anything about what happened on the 6th of December orally or did you write about this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after this ended?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, the 6th of December, and after the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me about what had happened, and I did not give any statements in writing or orally about that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Drljan.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you testified today that on 6th morning you were ordered by Captain Zec to go to Zarkovica. What time was this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10 past and 15 past 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you take steps to record that order that you were to convey to Captain Kovacevic in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not enter that particular piece of information into the war diary because I hurried up to Zarkovica, to find the driver, so that he would take me up there, and also to put on some warmer clothes because it was cold. But I do remember that order very well, because I had no reason to go to Zarkovica unless I had received orders to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But as you stated on Friday, all orders, all activities, matters relating to your forces, activities of the enemy forces, are all recorded in the war diary. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I said that all important events, woundings, killings, movements of troops, should be recorded in the logbook. But I did not say that the movements of a particular frigate captain who had received certain orders should be recorded in the logbook, although such an entry can be made as well. But it is not a mistake if this kind of entry is not made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The entry that you made at 1305, where you say: "The order of the command of the 9th VPS to Captain Kovacevic to cease firing on the town but to act only on the immediate vicinity of Srdj, has been transmitted," which is at page 70 of the war diary. At what time did you get that order from Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question to you is: At what time did you get this second order, or is it a reference to your previous order that you have recorded here at 1305?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not the same being repeated. The first order I received in the morning was to go straight there and to convey the order to Kovacevic, and here I'm being told to do it by telephone, via communications. So that's what I did. I wrote down when I conveyed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So this second time you telephoned Captain Kovacevic on Zarkovica and conveyed the order to him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So according to your testimony, you have now conveyed to Captain Kovacevic two orders prohibiting him from firing on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first order explicitly prohibited him from firing on the Old Town, and the second order only says the town, which means the entire town of Dubrovnik, including Gruz also, and other areas, but that he could only fire on Srdj. In my opinion, this was an order that was to ensure a cease-fire, only on Srdj, for as long as it took the forces to pull out. I conveyed what I had understood. But my understanding was that action would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So according to the second order, it's not only against the Old Town, but he has been ordered to cease fire against the entire Dubrovnik, except for Srdj? That is what the second order refers to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have it in writing. I believe that was the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And both these orders were given to you to be conveyed to Captain Kovacevic by Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first order in the morning was sent directly to me and I was in charge of going to Zarkovica. The second order was addressed to any officer at the forward command post who happened to be near the phone at the time. It could as well have been Kozaric or Sikimic or anyone else. Whoever answers the phone is told what the order is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question was the source of this order at that time, and even in the morning, was Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the morning when you were specifically asked to go to Zarkovica and convey the message to Captain Kovacevic, you were in fact asked this because you were a senior officer of the 9th VPS, in fact, at the level of lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First a major and then the colonel and lieutenant colonel. There were two senior officers there, and one lower-ranking officer, Sikimic, who at the time was captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, I'm asking you for your rank. I shall be grateful if you could confine your response to the question. My question was: You were being sent to Zarkovica to order Captain Kovacevic not to fire on the Old Town because of your senior rank. You were at the level of lieutenant colonel. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Captain Kovacevic necessarily was a subordinate officer to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about direct subordination, but certainly in terms of rank-wise, you were senior to, in terms of rank, to Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My rank was more senior, and that would have constituted a reason for a senior officer to go and to order what Admiral Jokic had ordered. But there was another reason why I was the one to go and not someone else. Namely, at the peacetime command of the Boka naval sector, I was working there, while Sikimic, for example, came.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, could you please confine your response to my question, because we are under time constraints. My question is about ranks. In terms of ranks, you were a senior officer, or your rank was senior to that of Captain Kovacevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so when you went to Zarkovica, in addition to your senior rank, you were also carrying an order from the command of the 9th VPS, instructing Captain Kovacevic not to fire on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you conveyed that order to Captain Kovacevic on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did convey it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And he clearly indicated to you that he understood your instructions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unequivocally and clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Within the next hour, while you observed, you said you saw two shells falling on the Old Town, a clear breach of the very orders you conveyed to Captain Kovacevic just within the hour?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw just one shell, as I said, some time ago, just one shell. There was one out-coming shell and then one incoming shell. In both cases, we are looking at a single shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, your -- what you have said previously has been recorded in the transcript, and what you said was that you observed two shells falling on the Old Town while you sat at that low wall and watched. So whether it's one or two, my point is: You conveyed to Captain Kovacevic an order from the command not to fire on the Old Town, and while you were yourself on Zarkovica, in your very presence, that order is breached. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you nevertheless stand there and watch for -- watched the activity for a while and then go back to Kupari and have your breakfast, in the face of that clear insubordination?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that one shell had fallen. After their shell had been fired. Now, if you could please find me a man anywhere on this planet who will turn a blind eye to such an attack where his own men might be killed. There's a position that's being fired from and now this man will resist returning fire. If you can find a man like that, and that was the reason that I did not pay attention, especially because we are looking at only one shell that was fired, a single shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let us not argue about the number of shells, Mr. Drljan, due to lack of time. But are you aware that attacking the Old Town was considered a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, but it's also a criminal act for any forces to be positioned inside it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please confine your response to my question. My question was as to whether you were aware as to --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in your presence, when an order prohibiting attack on the Old Town, which is considered a criminal act, is breached, why did you not take any steps to report that act of insubordination to a senior officer or the senior command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that when I came back to Kupari; however, neither the commander nor Zec were there, and I didn't know where they were. I asked at the forward command post about Zec's whereabouts, but I couldn't find him, because he was away somewhere, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To whom did you report it to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't report it to anyone. It wasn't my duty to report that to anyone, with the exception of Zec or Admiral Jokic. However, neither were present. I asked where they were, and when I was told that no one knew their whereabouts, I simply gave it up. I didn't tell anyone that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you observe a criminal act being committed in breach of orders which you personally conveyed to the subordinate officer, you don't take any steps at least to make an entry somewhere. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to inform Zec or Jokic, but I didn't find them. There was no one who had authority to give any order, nor did I have sufficient authority to order Kovacevic to cease fire. Because there was no firing after that. One shell had been fired. The shell fell, and there was no firing after that, at least not while I was present. A shell is fired at a single point in time, and then if there are no more shells following, there is nothing for me to do. But Jokic and Zec later did find out what had been done. It wasn't up to me. I didn't have sufficient authority to stop that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that more than one shell has been fired on the Old Town on 6 December from the positions of the 3rd Battalion? Did you find it out at least later on, if not within that one hour you were on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did find out later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in that context, did you take steps to file a report or even -- verbal report to any superior officer that you yourself was privy to the 3rd Battalion shelling the Old Town, albeit it being one shell that you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Kozaric, who wrote a report for Jokic, reporting on the activities that were undertaken on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you are aware that a report has been submitted to Admiral Jokic on the activities of the 3rd Battalion which were undertaken on the 6th of December, based on information that had been provided to the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, the operations centre submits a report to its superior commander. On that day, Kozaric was the one to write the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, considering your senior rank, when you returned to the operations centre from Zarkovica, did you take steps to inform the Croatian forces or any international observers of what you observed in the Old Town, that is to say, the mortar that you said you saw in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took no steps, because I did not have authority to take any steps on my own before conferring - that's anyone from the operations centre conferring - with the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you always follow or take permission from the commander or Chief of Staff before doing anything that you might think prudent?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on how difficult a task one is facing. In peacetime conditions, there are quite many things that I can do on my own. However, in wartime conditions, when human lives are at stake, on both sides, then it is not up to me to make these calls.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you consult the commander or the Chief of Staff when you decided to go to Bosanka in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you consult the commander or the Chief of Staff when you decided to go again to Zarkovica in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why did you remain on Zarkovica for one hour, having conveyed Captain Zec's order to Captain Kovacevic? Were you curious to observe and to see what was happening with regard to the Old Town? Is that why you perched yourself on that specific location overlooking the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, when I came there, I was not ordered to go back, nor was I given a deadline by which I should have been back from Zarkovica. So since no deadline had been set, I stayed and watched some things happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you saw Maljutkas being fired on the Old Town from Zarkovica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no Maljutkas there. I can't say there were none there. I'm just saying that I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were aware that there was Maljutka launchers on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that Maljutkas were a part of the weapons in possession of our forces, but not at Zarkovica. I really don't know whether they had Maljutkas at Zarkovica or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you don't know whether they had Maljutkas on Zarkovica. You didn't see, for instance, when you went to Zarkovica, Maljutka launchers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And apart from this one shell that you claim now - earlier on you said two - you didn't see any other mortar shells falling on the Old Town from JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, with the exception of that one shell. And I saw one of their shells. And I told you also that I had seen flashes of light behind the Orlando column. I never said two shells. I'm not sure why that was recorded, because that's just not right. They fired one shell. They pulled a mortar out, and soon after, our own shell fell on the Stradun. And then after that, I saw flashes of light behind the Orlando column. I'm talking about flashes of light because I'm not sure if it was the shells or where they fell. So that was my statement. That was my testimony, and that's precisely what I said. I'm not sure what and why it's reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, where exactly was this mortar on Stradun? You say you pointed a place. But could you identify that place by name from where you were or did you just see it somewhere on Stradun?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with street names in Dubrovnik. I know it more as a town. Even my own town, I don't know every single street. I know that the main street in Dubrovnik is called Stradun and that it was midway down the Stradun that a mortar came out and fired a single shell. After that, nearby, in approximately the same spot, our shell fell. Now, I can't give you the exact measures, nor am I familiar with the streets. The only street I am familiar with is the Stradun because that's the main street, and I know the Orlando column because that's a famous monument there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you saw this from Zarkovica, which means at approximately 2.500 to 3.000 metres away from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, I pointed out, if you remember, that there was a strong wind on that day and the weather was clear, visibility excellent. Even at 4.000 metres, you could tell that a mortar was firing, let alone 2.000 metres. It's only very easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you manage to determine what the calibre of that mortar was which was firing from within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How did you manage to pinpoint the exact location on the map, P13, which was shown to you by learned counsel? And you in fact placed the pointer and showed the exact position where the said mortar was, when in fact your only point of reference is that it's somewhere midway on Stradun? In such context, how did you manage to pinpoint the exactly location on the map?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this was interpreted at the time when I was answering a question by Defence counsel. It was midway down the street. I'm not sure if that was translated. I hope it was. I did say the first time around, halfway down the street, and then there was a circle that was drawn and then they wanted the exactly location. And I said: Well, hereabouts. They wanted the exactly location, but I can't give the exactly location. It's an approximation. I don't have the tools to determine the exact length of the street. I can only give you an approximate idea of the whereabouts of the impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it was roughly, you guessed the area, that's how you placed the pointer and indicated. You couldn't say the exactly location with certainty?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could do that. But there was a mortar on the Stradun. That's for sure. Whether it was ten metres to the left or ten metres to the right, I don't think that's really material.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the same manner in which you identified the locations you said you saw smoke emanating from? You pointed certain -- placed your pointer on the map and indicated certain positions, and by what you're saying, it presupposes that in relation to those two locations also you probably guessed.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you a rough idea of the whereabouts, because it has been 13 years since I looked on. However, I clearly remember that there was smoke there and that there was another building, also about midway down the Stradun, and that there was smoke coming out of that building's window and rising above the roof. This is something I can never forget. I may go wrong by the -- a dozen metres to the left or to the right, but there was smoke coming out; I'm sure about that. As well as about that other house burning where the colour of the smoke rising out was different, and this building was in a different part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a new subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It is still -- but if it's a convenient time for a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will take a break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, when you were sent to Zarkovica with the specific order instructing Captain Kovacevic to -- prohibiting him to fire on the Old Town, you had been sent at that hour because by this time, the 3rd Battalion had already been shelling the Old Town; isn't it? That is why you were specifically sent with an order instructing Captain Kovacevic not to fire on the Old Town; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. Because I had received the order in Kupari. I didn't see whether there was shelling or -- shelling or not, but I presume that's why they sent me up there. As long as I got this order, it means that shells were falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you started watching, or by the time you started watching the Old Town from the elevation, the Old Town had already been shelled, and in the midst of that activity, what you're saying is the people in the Old Town bring a mortar into Stradun, in clear vicinity of Zarkovica, and fired a mortar? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that a mortar had been pulled out and it fired one shell. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Pulled out of where?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a big entrance or a gate to a building. It's in fact a big wooden door covering or being positioned in the passage between two buildings. That's what we call house door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you could see this gate or door?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this gate was on the northern side of the Stradun or southern side of the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the southern side of Stradun, opposite the position where I was, because that's the part that I could see. The gates on the opposite side of the street I couldn't see because of the roofs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how long did it take to bring the mortar out, load it, and fire? What was the time period that this whole process took?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are you saying that a mortar was pulled out of a gate, placed on Stradun, a shell was loaded on, and the mortar was fired within a period of one minute?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only they were not loading the shell. You just drop it from above, and as soon as it reaches the bottom, it exploded immediately. It doesn't take more than five seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Drljan - perhaps an officer of your seniority should know - that a mortar cannot be fired from a hard surface, because the recoil -- there has to be a soft surface to absorb the recoil? Isn't that the case? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to shoot from a hard surface in exceptional cases. A soft surface is desirable, but if possible, to shoot from a hard surface. I'm not an artillery expert, but I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... permit me to tell you that there has been expert testimony led before this Trial Chamber where the experts have testified that a mortar cannot be fired from a hard surface, that if a mortar is to be fired from a hard surface, you have to prepare the surface with a soft substance to absorb the recoil. So an officer of your seniority obviously do not seem to know this fact [sic].

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it possible to place a rubber pad underneath so that the mortar was on the rubber pad instead of the cobblestone of the street?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, I'm not here to respond to your questions. But your testimony was that the mortar was pulled out of a gate placed on the Stradun and fired within one minute, which obviously presupposes there is no time to prepare the surface.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking for your response.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, mortars were placed, and that is what we heard through observation and saw for ourselves, that they had marked mortar positions where they had calculated firing elements at certain specific firing positions or targets on the opposite side. So they placed mortars immediately on such positions, fire the shell, and pull the mortar away. And as I said, it may fire one shell, but it cannot fire for a longer period of time. I presume, but I couldn't see from that distance, that they had placed some soft pad underneath --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Underneath the pedestal of the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You did not see such a thing; you could not see such a thing from your distance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see. But I could see that mortar had fired, and that's what I ascertain here with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where did it fire to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direction of north, somewhere in the direction of Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know that the buildings on the northern side of Stradun are very high?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not that high so as to preclude a shell from passing over them and attacking other positions, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So your testimony is that the particular shell was fired at Srdj and not Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on Srdj. Not a single shell fell on Zarkovica for as long as Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this whole process could be also observed along with you by the units positioned on Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could. If anyone was paying attention, if they were not busy with their own activities, if they just watched in that direction. But if they turned away, they maybe could not have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you know -- do you know how a Maljutka is operated, that a Maljutka is a projectile which is guided by the operator to the target, and as such, a precision weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And therefore, if a mortar was visible on Stradun for that period, it could have been easily neutralised with one Maljutka projectile, isn't that the case, from Zarkovica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been neutralised, but the mortar was pulled back inside immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, don't you think it would be quite risky for a mortar to be placed on Stradun in full vicinity of Zarkovica, especially considering that Zarkovica has Maljutka launchers? Won't it be considered as suicidal?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their principle was: Fire and find shelter immediately. And that is a possible concept.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said you observed the shell from the OG positions, 2nd Operational [sic] position or the 3rd Battalion positions being fired on the Old Town. Didn't you consider your presence there, your continuous presence there and even your subsequent visit there, could be considered as encouragement by those units towards the activities, especially considering that you did not take any measures to have the order not to fire on the Old Town implemented and enforced?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very accurate when I said that I had been sent by the warship Captain Zec upon Admiral Jokic's order to convey the order, not to undertake any measures. While I was there leaning on the wall, another order could have arrived that I had not been aware of, and it was not my place to interfere with the progress of the struggle in order to avoid bearing influence that I possibly could take blame later for. So I didn't want to interfere. I just did what I had been ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you came back to the operations centre, did you report about what you observed in the Old Town, that is, this particular mortar that fired and the flashes you saw? Did you report it to the operations centre or your command?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not duty operations officer, nor was it my duty to report. Reports are written towards the end of the day, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, please. I'm not talking about written reports. Did you report, either verbally or by just -- in a casual way, did you report to anybody that you saw a mortar in the Old Town and you saw these flashes that you spoke of today?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told that to Sikimic and Kozaric, as soon as I entered, and I told them that for their information. Kozaric was already on the phone. He was receiving orders. He was very busy. I don't know if he had heard me or not. I believe he did. I said that I saw a mortar and that our forces hit the Stradun with one shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did the shell do? Did that shell damage the Stradun or the structures around Stradun? What did that JNA shell that you observed falling on Stradun do in terms of damage?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I took my binoculars and I didn't see any damage, because this was a very hard surface made of stone, and the shell dispersed. Whether there were any broken windows in the vicinity, I couldn't see that, because one couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So a shell falls or impacts on a particular point and you don't observe any damage at all? That's what you're saying here?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. I didn't notice any damage, because it fell on a hard, stone surface, and it burst into fragments. It fell right on the Stradun, did not hit any of the buildings. And I said to myself, "That was a good hit." Because that is the position where formerly the Croatian mortar had been. And after that, this mortar never appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you are in fact -- you were condoning this particular attack on the Old Town, when you said, "That was a good hit."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that from the point of view of the precision of the hit. Maybe the Croats would characterise that as a good hit. That did not mean that I condoned it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ensure when you got back to the operations centre that the information you conveyed to Kozaric and the other person was recorded in the war diary, the logbook?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was recorded in the war log, certain operations carried out by units. And I didn't think it appropriate or necessary to record one mortar hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is with regard to the mortar that you observed in the Old Town. Did you ensure that this information was recorded?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that to Kozaric, and this information should have been included in the evening report. I presume that's what happened. I never checked anyone who was in charge or whose rank was superior to mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D96, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So while that document is being shown - and that is the war diary you've already taken a look at - would you please examine the entries for 6 December and tell us as to whether you can find a single entry as to the presence of a mortar in the Old Town on 6 December. Now, you testified that all enemy activity, enemy positions and such information is recorded in the war diary. So that presupposes that this item of information should be in fact recorded in the war diary, if in fact it was true.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was true. Now, why it was not recorded in the war log, I don't know, because I did not have the war log on me to register this as soon as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, as an operations officer yourself, as a person who himself has made entries in this war diary, and as a person who claims to have seen this mortar in the Old Town himself, would it not have logically followed that you'd have this piece of information entered in this war diary if it was true?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this before midday, when I returned, the logbook had already been filled for that period of time. I said this to Kozaric. He could have made that entry, but he didn't. I did not deem it appropriate to record something in the war logbook that had happened several hours before that, because you can see that all the different times are there in proper sequence. And it reflects everything that happened on that day. Not every little detail, but, anyway, there is an entry where it says how many shells were fired from a particular position of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you say that all entries are entered in chronological sequence and that's why you could not have this particular information entered into the war diary. Would you please examine the entries relevant to 6 December. And I'm drawing your attention to the entry on page 67 at 7.15. Do you see that at 7.15, one hour, 15 minutes afterwards, there is an entry to this effect. I'm referring to page 67. On page 67, there is an entry at 7.15: "Positions on Strincjera were hit from Srdj around 6 hours with Zoljas and MB-82." So here is an entry made at 7.15 which relates to an event that took place, or occurred at 6.00 in the morning. And it has been entered after three entries or -- I'm sorry, two entries which have been made --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- with regard to events that happened much after. So your explanation about logical sequence or chronological sequence does not seem to hold in view of this document itself, isn't it, Mr. Drljan? In fact, there was no prohibition or no bar whatsoever for you to enter that item of information, at whatever time, in this war diary, if in fact it was true?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing prevented me from entering that information, even later on, subsequently. But I did not deem it appropriate to make that kind of entry, referring to one shell only. You see that I did not refer to their firing of a shell or our firing of a shell, neither. Because on that day, there were so many shells that were exchanged between our side and the Croatian side that this one shell was not all that important. That's why I did not deem it necessary to make that kind of entry subsequently. I just said what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, can you please turn to page 61. That is in the entry in relation to 4th December 1991. At 1833, you made an entry that on Srdj a transporter was noticed. "No contact." That's your entry. That's your entry, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravkovic told me about that. I wrote down what he reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so such information that a transporter is noticed on Srdj is deemed important enough to get into this document, but a mortar observed in the Old Town in the course of combat is not deemed important to get into this document? That's what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this piece of information with the obligation to write it down, because that could have been a preparation for something, I don't know what for. But anyway, we were duty-bound to record every piece of information we received by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D65. Let that document be there. D65, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Drljan, you said that it's possible that this information could have got into the report, a report perhaps submitted for the day. Could you please examine this document that has just been given to you. I appreciate that you may not have seen this before. It is a document sent?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't this document until now. And I've already said that it is possible, which is not to say that it was recorded too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please note that this document, which is a report sent by the forward command post Kupari to the First Administration for General Simonovic, titled "action report of the 3rd Battalion on Srdj, 6 December 1991."
