There is no reference -- and this document, Mr. Drljan, is a document which has been tendered by the Defence in evidence. It does not contain a single reference to any weapons in the Old Town on 6 December 1991. Do you notice that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave. We have already had a discussion with regard to this document once, in terms of the heading that goes above the words "Simonovic," et cetera, and we all noted that there was a mistake in the translation. And I thought that we had all ascertained that. But it seems to me that my learned friend did not note that. So I would like to draw her attention once again to the type of report that this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, would you please read out the title of the report, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Report on the action of the 3rd Battalion, 472nd Naval Landing Brigade." This is a mistake. This is not motorised brigade. It is naval brigade. "Against Srdj on the 6th of December, 1991." That's the name -- that's the heading of the document, rather. Is that what you wanted?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It should be report on the action of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... report on the action of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Should it be -- should it be corrected in that manner? Not naval brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a naval landing brigade, not a motorised brigade. I know that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let's not argue on that, Mr. Drljan. Let's move on. Now, your allegation that you saw a mortar in the Old Town on 6 December is not recorded either in the war diary, D96, nor in this report, D --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend is saying something to the witness that is inaccurate. I would like to draw your attention to page 2 of this report, line 7 in B/C/S. There is a sentence that reads: "Until the beginning of the attack at 6.00 -- before the attack at 6.00, our forces were fired at by 82-millimetre mortars, and this mortar fire went on until 1430 hours." Fire from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point is, Your Honour, that there is no reference to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on as you will, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going back, Mr. Drljan. I put it to you that your claim of seeing a mortar in the Old Town, Stari Grad, on 6 December 1991 is not recorded in the war diary, D96, for the record, or this order for the 6th December, which is -- I beg your pardon. The report on the activities of the 3rd Battalion on the 6th December, and that is because there was no such mortar on the 6th December that you saw. It is an incorrect assertion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just intervene briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this an objection to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, look, I've mentioned before: If you're making objections about the evidence, one counsel does that, not changing. You have often been allowed, and reasonably, to intervene where there's a witness of Mr. Rodic's when it's a matter of translation in the record. But if there is an objection, it should be made by Mr. Rodic, as this is his witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please respond to my question. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's an objection pending.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the essence of this objection is that my learned friend says that there is no evidence that would corroborate that there was firing from the Old Town of Dubrovnik in the reports that were made. Could my learned friend please look at D62. That is only one of the exhibits that has to do with this particular matter regarding the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. It is not proper for counsel to refer to other items of evidence before a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point being made is that you are misquoting or misidentifying the evidence, the state of the evidence, to the witness in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My question was merely that the fact that this item of information is not recorded in the war diary, nor this particular report, that is D96 and D65, is because there were -- the witness's assertion that there was a mortar in the Old Town on 6 December is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what's being put against you is that there are other documents which do record firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I don't intend to waste time on this. I will withdraw the question and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Drljan, you testified of seeing a flash behind the tower. Could you please name the tower again, the tower or the pillar behind from -- behind which you saw a flash.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orlando column, the Orlando column.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what's the height of this column?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps about ten metres, six, perhaps even less. I don't know exactly. I don't know exactly, but it is high enough. A few people can stand behind it without being seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what's the width of this column?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how many people could stand behind the column? When you say a few people, about five people, six people, could stand behind them shoulder to shoulder without being seen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two people can stand there without being seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you saw a flash from behind this pillar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few flashes. In certain intervals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were these flashes -- how wide were the flashes in terms of width?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were big enough to be seen from behind the pillar. I could see them behind the pillar. Say half a metre or 70 centimetres. The flash could be seen perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You mean you could see the flash about half a metre extending outside the pillar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Lengthwise half a metre. There is length and there is width. So the length was about 50 centimetres behind the pillar, and that's where it could be seen. You see the flash and then it's no longer there, quite naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But you did not see a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it had to be some sort of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What time of the day was this? What time was it when you saw this flash?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about half past 8.00, 8.30 or thereabouts. Don't take my word for it, though. I wasn't exactly looking at my watch. I was thinking about other things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 8.30 in the morning, daylight?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you in fact said it was a very clear day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you know that -- how do you know that -- I beg your pardon. I'll withdraw that. How do you know that this flash was in fact muzzle flash and not really a flash emanating from explosion? Have you seen that when a shell impacts on a particular surface, there's an explosion and there's a huge flash? You would have seen it, considering the number of years you served in the military, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have seen it, yes. When a shell falls, in addition to the flash of light that lasts for a moment, it also raises a lot of dust Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond around where it impacts. It causes damage to the walls, to the pavement, and there's a lot of dust all around. But there was no dust around that particular flash of light. Therefore, it was only weapon firing, but not a shell falling. These two are very easy to distinguish, and there is no doubt about this. When our shell fell on the Stradun, I recognised it immediately for what it was, our shell, because there was dust in the air around where it fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, don't you know, being an officer with your experience, that muzzle flash cannot be seen during the daytime? Muzzle flash from mortars and artillery cannot be seen during the daytime. Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you see a match being lit at a distance of 20 metres in daylight? Just a small match I'm talking about. Of course you can see it, and the flash too can be seen. I assert this with full responsibility. I did see that flash, and yes, it can be seen in daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, I'm about to show you two photographs of mortars being fired and photographed at the point the shell leaves the barrel. And these photographs show what we call the muzzle flash, which should be visible during the day. Mr. Drljan, you just said, and I think the words you used were you were saying it with a sense of responsibility that you saw a flash, that you could see a flash or you could see the muzzle flash.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the objection, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to make this sort of assertion, such as the one put forward by my learned friend and colleague, I don't think these photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you at that point. The cross-examination is proper, and I don't want your objection to be providing answers to the witness. Carry on, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not to say that you may not want to put something about it in re-examination. But at this point, the cross-examination is proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, don't these two photographs show that one cannot observe a muzzle flash at the point of firing, in mortar and artillery fire, but contrary to what you stated?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a flame here behind the shell itself. Can you see it behind the shell? I didn't see the barrel, but I saw a flame. You can see here clearly that there is a trace of fire that will disappear quickly. You can see it just behind the shell. It's a flame.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what you are telling this Trial Chamber is that you can see a flame on these photographs which is perhaps a type of flash that you saw on 6 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Even here you can see, just behind the shell, there is a flame which is about to disappear, because it goes away very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So I do not see it, Mr. Drljan, but perhaps what you can see in these photographs is what you saw on 6 December.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is that a possibility, it's actually true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this in fact, whatever you saw, was at a distance of about approximately 3.000 metres from an elevation and behind the pillar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This event took place behind the pillar, and you can see the flame clearly. I've been doing that for 17 years. I'd sailed for 17 years, and my eyesight is very sharp, because I had trained my eyesight by sailing. When I look at something that's that sort of distance, I just can't go wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Considering your experience, do you recognise the artillery in the picture which has a blue tinge? Do you recognise that weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that is a picture of a mortar firing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you speak up a little, your response. Can you speak up, because the interpreter did not get your response.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mortar while firing a shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the other picture, the green -- the picture with the green tinge, what is that weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that is a mortar firing a shell?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also at the time, also. It's not clearly visible, but I think it's a mortar firing a shell. The image is a bit blurred, but yes, it is a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May these two photographs be tendered in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These exhibits are P219.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, now you testified about the war diary, and that all important activities, matters relating to your forces, matters relating to enemy activity, important events, are all recorded in the war diary. You said that on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you testified that in fact these entries are made for purposes of compiling combat reports?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So at the end of the day, or at some stage, the officer who compiles the daily combat reports summarises the entries and submits a report based on the entries in the war diary. Is that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not only the war log or from the war log. You can enter other information that is obtained or reported by commanders who come in to report. Even unbeknownst to us, if something is happening, then such events too can be recorded. So commanders come in to report. They tell us about what they had been doing during the day, and that too can be entered in a report. However, a report never contains everything, but only the most essential things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My point was that whilst the war diary could include all information, what the commanders inform and all of the important events, the entries in the war diary are used for compiling the combat reports. Isn't that the way? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So as such, the information in combat reports should correspond to the entries in the war diary, necessarily; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such information as is recorded from the war log and transferred into a report must be identical in terms of their content. But that doesn't necessarily mean that everything is copied from the war log and goes into the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What other sources are there to support a combat report, if it's not the war diary? There has to be some other document being maintained at an operations centre which has a record of the activities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, in the evening hours, commanders of subordinate units arrive and report each on their own respective units, and what happened during the day. Their statements are not recorded in the war log but can be included in the daily combat report, as well as possible orders that came in, if any orders came in. Information is obtained from those two to be included in combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And where do commanders come and compile these reports at? At the operations centre, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations centre. There is a special room there. They sit down and report, each man for himself. They report on what was done during a certain day and what the activities were for each of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you or an operations officer is on duty and you receive some important information, you would necessarily include that in the war diary? And I'm not referring to your visit on Zarkovica. I'm referring if you were in fact on duty at the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am on duty at the operations centre and I receive important, I emphasis, important information, I will be certain to record it in the war log.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if, for instance, when you were on duty, you got a telephone call or received a telephone call from the General Staff, which is undoubtedly important, you would record it in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if, for instance, General Kadijevic from Belgrade telephoned you and asked you to immediately contact or establish contact with the commander of the 9th VPS, you would necessarily record that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly that would be recorded, and I would establish contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this would be the case with regard to all operations centres, I presume, the procedure you've just mentioned with regard to the operations centre in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That's at least the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If any combat orders were received by you to pass on to any units when you were in fact the duty-officer, you would have that recorded in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have recorded that briefly, a combat order, such-and-such number, forwarded to such-and-such a person. I would not write out the whole thing, because the combat order is there and it can be attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please peruse the war diary, Mr. Drljan. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please peruse page 59, and those are the entries for the 4th. And there, at 7.50, and on page 60, the entry for 1600 hours, there are entries relating to weather forecasts. Now, was it a weather monitoring unit that provided this information to the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The weather forecast could be received from the radio station that was on the coast. In our case, that was Bar, B-a-r. Or else, for it to be recorded, it could have been received from the TV weather forecast or the one broadcast all over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were steps taken to have the units informed of these weather forecasts, units involved in combat operations? Not by you. I'm saying in the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This forecast from the VPS Boka was forwarded only to the ships that were about to set sail or already at sea or had received orders to set sail. So this forecast was mainly required for the ships and their sailing. It wasn't relevant and important for and units deployed on the land.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 61, the entry at 1815. Now, that is an entry that has been made by you, and it has been -- that information is provided to you by frigate Captain Jeremic. And there's a reference there to the --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There's a reference there to the effect that he did not want to attack today. Whom are you referring to, or do you know what that information is all about? Which attack does that refer to, and whom are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me first to read this before I answer your question. This was a message from the Croatian army, their internal message, intercepted by frigate Captain Jeremic, with one of our radio stations. This refers to the front. That was somewhere near Ston, which is very far from Dubrovnik, and this front was over 50 kilometres away, and that is where our forces and the Croatian forces were in contact in that particular area. Because Dubrovnik was surrounded, and we proceeded further on down the highway, and probably their intention was to attack our forces and to get as close to Dubrovnik as possible, that is, the forces that were there. But this was very far away from us -- I mean from Dubrovnik. And this man was dismissed because he didn't want to proceed with the attack, and another man was brought to replace him. Both men were from the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a comprehensive cease-fire agreement that was to be concluded on 6 December?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know until the evening, when I heard -- on the 6th of December, when I heard that an agreement on truce was about to be concluded. But I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you -- on 5th December, you did not know that there was a cease-fire agreement to be concluded on 6 December? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's my statement. Frigate Captain Jeremic was a liaison officer. He was in charge of that. And we were not informed every time a negotiation was going on, unless we were required to provide certain things for the negotiations. Otherwise, since on that occasion we were not required to provide anything --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, would you please turn to page 66. That is the entries relating to 5th December. And I'm referring to the entries at 1940 and 1942. Those are entries made by you, isn't it? The entry at 1940 -- who has entered the entry at 1940, which is just below the entry that you have made? Your name is in the remark column against the entry just before that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So who made the entry at 1940?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1940, I suppose that it was done by Captain Dzelebdzic because this is neither Sikimic's nor Kozaric's because this is neither Sikimic's nor Kozaric's handwriting, nor mine. So he could not have made those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 57, line 2, the witness said Captain Dzelebdzic, not Kovacevic, as it says in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Drljan, that just below the entry made by you, the two entries at 1940 and 1942, clearly indicate that there is a cease-fire agreement to be concluded the next day? Yet being an officer of your seniority, on 5th December, you were not aware of an important event as a comprehensive cease-fire agreement which was to be concluded the next day, when it was in fact recorded in the very war diary that you yourself made entries in?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was entered by Captain Dzelebdzic and received from the frigate Captain Handzijev. So it came from the main command post for our information only. Generally, no officer from the forward command post took part in those negotiations. Therefore, I have nothing to do with this entry, and I was not interested in it, pending the reaching of the agreement. So it was -- a peace agreement was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you were not interested in learning about a comprehensive cease-fire? You say that you were not interested in it. Is that what you're saying? An officer of your seniority would not be interested in a comprehensive cease-fire that's to be brought about the very next day.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a laughable question, with all due respect, but I find it ridiculous. We were all interested in cease of fire. If I were to decide, I would not have attacked Dubrovnik at all. But I would not dwell on this further. I was not interested in this entry because it preceded the negotiations. I was more interested in the outcome of negotiations and for ensuring the Argos to sail out of the harbour and that's what we secured. It set sail and our ships did not attack it. That was the critical point for us. What Jeremic and the others were going to negotiate about, we would only learn later on. But of course I was interested in peace and things. And I find this to be a provocative question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 62. And I'm referring you to the entry -- entries for 5th December 1991. That's entry for 9.50. There's a reference to the 9th VPS command forwarding an act of the General Staff and indicating that the vessel Cap Africa should be permitted to enter the port of Dubrovnik and remain there from 5th December to 8th December; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ship.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that is a foreign vessel, isn't it, a civilian foreign vessel?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a French cargo ship, a ferry, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Additionally, at page 65, the entry at 1745, refers to a dialogue between the 9th VPS and the ICRC team to meet on 6 December to carry out some installation work.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, it was possible to let a foreign civilian vessel enter into the port of Dubrovnik and arrange meeting with ICRC teams on the 6th December, because at this stage there was a cease-fire in place and no combat activity was anticipated on 6 December, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about the activities that were to happen on the 6th of December. And this particular vessel, called Cap Africa, had not yet entered the Dubrovnik port.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 64. The entry at 1441, there is a reference to re-subordination of 1LM and 1TC. So you please indicate as to what 1LM and 1TC is.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what an LM is, and TC is I think a territorial company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So some units are being re-subordinated, some technical units being re-subordinated from the VP -- I beg your pardon. From the fleet to the 9th VPS here, isn't it, particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this refers to naval units, this is a land sweeper, probably, LM, and a TC is a torpedo boat. So after I've read the whole passage, it seems that they're referring to naval vessels.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So clearly, the fact that these particular facilities are being subordinated from the fleet to the 9th VPS indicates that the fleet is not within the subordination of the 9th VPS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The fleet was re-subordinated to the command of the 9th Naval District.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. My point is: This entry indicates clearly that the fleet is not subordinated to the 9th Naval Sector. The issue of re-subordination of units from the fleet to the 9th Naval Sector does not arise if in fact the fleet was within the 9th Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please read in that entry, right at the bottom, there is a statement by the fleet commander: "I am unaware of the consent of the KVPO that you were given in relation to the use of the fleets' ships. 1424 hours." This is a message from fleet commander to Captain Zec, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't this a message to Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must read it. Yes, yes, it is addressed to Captain Zec, and he was the Chief of Staff of the naval sector. The fleet commander, I cannot Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond tell you now who the commander was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the fleet commander is telling Captain Zec that he's not aware of some information or consent given by the naval military district for certain activities? Isn't that what the fleet commander is indicating there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just first read before I answer. This document had been sent to Captain Zec because previously, probably, somebody requested the replacement for the ships that had been at sea for a long time. It says here 80 days and to replace those ships and give some time to the crews for rest. They were asking for one minesweeper and one torpedo boat to replace those vessels that had been assigned up until then. Their duty was to escort convoys and carry out other tasks as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the reference to KVPO there is the naval district; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it approves re-subordination of these two vessels.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, would you please indicate: In the war diary, which is before you, apart from the entries which is made by time, there is an overview of events for the day. Who makes these overview of events in the war diary?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The review of daily events in a war log -- are you referring to this? So the daily review is essentially a daily report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And so whoever who makes these overview of events for the day goes through the entries and summarises the events, or the entries, into an overview. That's necessarily what an overview of the events is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please turn to the overview for 6 December, that is, the page before page 67. Now, there is -- page before page 67.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Summary of events of the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that summary, it starts off from 0010 to 0600 hours. The enemy has opened machine-gun and sniper fire on our positions at Strincjera. From 0600 to 0745, 82-millimetre fire was opened from Srdj, Lazaret, and H. Neptun on Strincjera. Until then, shells from handle. Non-stop mortar fire is coming from Hotel Libertas, Babin Kuk, and from Velika Petka. 1120 hours, 120-millimetre fire is still continuing on Srdj. Could you please turn the page and examine the entries for 6 December 1991. And isn't it the case that there isn't a single entry there on -- for the 6th December which supports that particular passage?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This summary of events was made by Kozaric, but only after receiving reports by commanders at the forward command post. In this long series of events that took place on that date, the commanders and company commanders were not able to report all the events to be entered into the war logs. They just recorded them in their notebooks, and when they came in the evening, they reported how many shells were fired, who fired from where, et cetera. So in the evening, they provided more accurate information, and that is why Kozaric compiled this overview; otherwise, this kind of overview is not made on a normal day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How do you know that, sir? How do you know that --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because not -- for no other day did we make a review. That was the most important single event in the period, and that is why this overview was made. Because not all the events and incidents could have been recorded in the war log. The commanders were busy on their positions, respective positions. They just noted them down in their notebooks. They didn't want to waste time by telephoning us at the time. Because their main preoccupation was to render command duties to all those who were involved in that struggle. And in the evening, they were able to provide more precise information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when these commanders came and reported to Kozaric, were you present? Is that how you know all this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that information as an officer, as a professional officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please, my question to you is: Were you present when these commanders came and reported to Kozaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: First say yes or no, and then please explain.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present, because when a man is appointed to be in charge of the briefing, he is the only person present, and the commanders are present. The others are not needed and are not present. Therefore, unless specific orders are issued to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So do you know, then, from some other source that on 6 December evening, commanders - and when you say commanders, commander of the 3rd Battalion, is that whom you're referring to - was present reporting to Kozaric as to what happened during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But I was not present, and I cannot make any claims as to what he had reported.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know as to whether the company commanders also came with the 3rd Battalion commander and reported to Kozaric on the evening of 6 December? Is that how this information came by?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During his testimony, the witness did not state anywhere that on the 6th of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, thank you. I get the drift of your objection. The question that's put is clear and can be answered, independently of what earlier evidence might have been given. Carry on, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please respond, Mr. Drljan. Do you know, in addition to the commander of the 3rd Battalion, the company commanders of the 3rd Battalion, were they present at whatever place reporting to Kozaric about the day's events? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember. Usually company commanders report to the commander of the battalion and then he, in turn, reports to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So who are the commanders? You said in the plural. Who are the commanders who reported to Kozaric that you mentioned earlier, in addition to the 3rd Battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What commanders are you referring to? It's not commanders in the sense of commandeers, leaders of particular units that reported to Kozaric. It was commanders, "komandante," that reported to him. There is a major difference involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to when you said that someone reported to Kozaric, which led to this -- summary in the war diary? You said the 3rd Battalion commander. In addition to that, who else reported to Kozaric? Do you know that? Because you said it with such certainty. That is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said with great certainty who was supposed to be there to report. I did not see that, because I was not there. I went to my room, because I was not invited to this briefing. And it's battalion commanders or detachment commanders who are supposed to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So apart from the 3rd Battalion commander, who else was supposed to be there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one. No one. No one from his unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How do you know this? Who told you that somebody reported to Kozaric that evening, which led to this overview being compiled?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you that Captain Kovacevic was supposed to collect all information from his company commanders, to write them down in his notebook, to come to the forward command post himself and report to Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D64 and D61.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, in the interests of time, I will ask you questions about both these documents at once. Would you please quickly peruse these two documents, which are combat reports submitted by Captain Zec. And do you note that the assertions in D64 about firing from the region of -- or from the area of the Old Town is not in the war diary. There are no entries which support --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. The Defence has not provided us with an English translation of this document still. This is a document put to Admiral Jokic. We are just struggling with this document. I'm referring to D64. If I may have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you further questions after this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Just about three or four questions. But if it's an appropriate time to take a break, afterwards I would take at the most about five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it might be better that way. It would allow the witness to finish reading the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then you can collect your thoughts for a speedy finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm getting very concerned at the time being taken with each witness by both Defence and Prosecution counsel. We are falling behind with every witness at the moment. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I made a mistake when I referred to the Exhibit number D64. It was actually D62, but during the break, with the assistance of the registrar, we did get the correct exhibit to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: D62 and D61 you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I didn't have my microphone on, I'm sorry. It's D62 and D61 that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, have you had an opportunity to go through these documents?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In document dated 5th December 1991, D61, the first paragraph refers to firing from enemy positions. Now, do you find in the war diary, D96, in the entries relating to 5th December 1991, any entry which corresponds to that particular report? That is a report on firing by enemy forces on 5th December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There is no entry that corresponds to that report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2355. Can I just have a moment to go through this, please. 2355 on the 5th, where Kovacevic says that he had come under fire, and the answer was that he should refrain from firing back. That's 2355. During the day, no fire was being opened, according to the log, at least, but fire was opened later on in the evening. Page 66, 2355.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But Mr. Drljan, the report D61 is filed at 1700 hours on 5th December 1991, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please not give me the document number, because the number is not stated on my copy of the document. Just give me the date and the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The report dated 5th December 1991 by Captain Zec, which refers to firing by enemy forces is compiled at 1700 hours, isn't it? And there is no --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues]... entry in the war diary which supports that report. That's my point. Could you please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of the time recorded, but probably Kozaric, who wrote the report, and the report was signed by Zec, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, my question was that there are no corresponding entries to the war diary. Please confine your response to my question.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no corresponding entry, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the evening report -- please allow me to finish answering. That day, commanders came in to report on the previous day, and probably they did before this report was written. They didn't do it by phone during the day while there was firing, but rather, they said it in the evening, when they came over. Therefore, it was an oral report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the document dated 6 December 1991, which is submitted by Captain Milan Zec. In that report, in the first paragraph, there is a reference to fire from Stradun region, as well as the old city port.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what you said before. That's what you claimed I didn't say, but I did say it, and it was recorded, and I told Kozaric orally as soon as I came.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you please let me finish my question. I'm on time constraint. And this document, D62, which contains the assertion to firing from the Old Town, or the region of the Old Town and the old city port, is not supported by any entry in the war diary for 6 December 1991. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No entry. But, as I said, I orally told Kozaric, as soon as I came, that I had seen a mortar positioned on the Stradun and that I had seen firing, or rather, a flame behind the Orlando column, which is near the Old Town harbour, and this is how he recorded it. He didn't record it in the logbook, but he did include it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D105, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, do you note that this order to control weapons is issued pursuant to -- or in keeping with the resolution passed by the Security Council of the United Nations, the UN Security Council? That's indicated in paragraph 2 of the document. Do you note that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do notice that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Drljan, while we still have D62 in front of us, it's the regular combat report of the command of the 9th VPS dated the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. There is no reference to this document being a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would respectfully suggest it's in the heading. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, do you have the report in front of you, and can you please open the logbook, the war logbook also, and can you please, first of all, look between page 66 of the war log and page 67. It's the page containing a handwritten summary of events.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the section that was marked in pen -- in pencil, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Circled?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where they're talking about the firing positions of the mortars at Lazareti, the firing positions of mortars at the Neptun Hotel, firing positions of mortars at Nuncijata, firing positions at Nuncijata Sustjepan and the number of shells that were fired by JNA units. And can you please look at point 2, item 2 of the regular combat report, Exhibit D62, to see if these data from the logbook were reflected here.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the positions and the number of shells that were actually fired?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just another thing that needs clarifying. The columns in the war log in D96, the boxes, the section that was divided up and where the tables had been entered for -- to contain entries, is that on the right-hand side of the log?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this, please, these entries.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. All the pages. You have tables that are drawn, lines are drawn to contain tables for entries and remarks to be entered. Is that on the right-hand page of the notebook that actually contains the war log?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is indeed the right-hand page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the page in between, the one that is a copy and contains a summary of events? Is that a blank page beside the right-hand page that is used possibly for these entries?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the summary pertains to the entire day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That's very well. Can you tell me about item 1, point 1, the enemy, regular combat report in the log, the war log, D96, at 0715, is there any reference to Zoljas and 82-millimetre mortars at about 6.00 firing at positions on Strincjera from Srdj? Is there any reference to that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So is there anything in the logbook, a reference to firing --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On Strincjera or against Strincjera, the position there.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strincjera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At 0715 hours.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoljas and 82-millimetre mortars around 0600 hours, positions on Strincjera were hit from Srdj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, please. Between page 69 of the logbook and page 70, therefore, a copy of a blank page that was written on --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It says the 6th of December, 1992, dead. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were the names of those who had been killed and wounded entered in the regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the regular combat report, D61, dated the 5th of December. Do you have the document in front of you, D61? The date is the 5th of December. And can you please keep it in front of you. Do you have the regular combat report, D61, dated the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the war log between page 63 and page 64 again. We find the copy of that blank page, the left-hand page, from the war log. Again, there is a box made in pencil here and the reference is to 1500 hours to 1530 hours, Pobrezje, Solitudo, fire; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: 1530 to 1600, Zarkovica, Bosanka, Strincjera?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: 1100 to 1200 hours, Bosanka, Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can certain entries also be made on the left-hand side of the log?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at item 1, point 1 of the regular combat report, D61, is there any reference there to a French ship called Cap Africa?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at the war log, the entries related to the 5th of December. Can any of the entries be in reference to the Cap Africa ship 0813, 0840, 0955?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 0830, that is a reference to the ship because the location is given. 0840 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: 0840, that's it being identified, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not enumerating everything, but, for example, 1025 --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1025, Stojadinovic, Cap Africa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You don't need to go through it. You don't need to read out. Just tell me if it's a reference to the ship.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The next page, at 1145?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please also look at -- for instance, on page 65, the entry made at 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We don't need the Exhibit D61 any more. I would kindly ask the witness to be given the Prosecution Exhibit P219. The witness, please keep the log with you. If you make a comparison between these two images, at first glance, do you think that the weather and geographical conditions in one image is identical to those in the other image? Just at first glance.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they are, only one of the images is more blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where the green is a dominant colour?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So would you say that it is more blurred? In which specific part of the photograph with respect to the barrel of the mortar is this blurred part?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is above this man who is bending over and around the shell itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does it go -- this blurred section, does it go from the muzzle of the mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Because in this picture, we cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Are the soldiers next to the mortar, are all away from the muzzle of the barrel?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, relatively speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at both photographs, is the distance between the shell and the muzzle of the barrel, is there a distance there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the distance on the right-hand side photograph; however, I don't see it on the left-hand side photograph, because I can't see the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me help you with this. The soldier, not the one whose back is turned towards you but the one facing you, between the two helmets, can you see?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see some barrels there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the barrels?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Above this soldier facing me, a barrel should be somewhere behind his back. If you extend the trajectory of the shell, but I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the flash lasts when a mortar is fired?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make an estimate. It's just a part of a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need this photograph any longer. Tell me: Do you know approximately what is the distance between Zarkovica and the Old Town as the crow flies? If you can make an estimate; if not, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2.000 metres, roughly speaking. It's not difficult to calculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drljan, what is a regular combat report as a document? What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a document, it represents a basic document for a particular and specific day, in which all important information, activities of all units are entered, I mean units on the ground, including all other significant reports that are received or orders that are received, orders issued and conveyed, and all movements in this particular case of ships. In a word, all the pertinent events that need to be recorded, for example, the number of the wounded, the injured, and the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Based on what information is the regular combat report compiled?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is compiled based on daily reports sent by units and on the basis of reports submitted by unit commanders in the evening when they come for a debriefing session. These are main sources for this kind of report. So a log is used. Everything that has been received as information is being recorded, and that includes oral reports given by commanders during debriefing. It has its certain established form.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Drljan, that, so to say, the two main sources of information for compiling a regular combat report are reports submitted by unit commanders, plus the information received from the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information received at the operations centre from units or commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Besides that, a regular combat report can include intelligence information as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please give the witness Exhibit D96 again. Mr. Drljan, will you please look at page 66 of the war log.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you about these entries at 1940 and 1942.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me -- please first read these entries. Just read it to yourself. You don't need to read them out loud. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me: At -- in the 1940 entry and 1942 entry, is there a word "cease-fire" there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are there words "signed agreement," or "agreement on truce."

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please look, the 2012 entry in the log, which is immediately after these previous two.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this imply that the requests by the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik were not complied with, who asked a ship route, Dubrovnik ship -- Dubrovnik to be established and for the works on the water pump to be commenced on the 12th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The command of the 9th VPS expressed here that they could not comply with those requests --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Fair comment, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm just trying to make it quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please read out loud the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We are ready to solve this issue shortly, which will primarily depend on the results of the negotiations to be held in Cavtat on the 6th of December, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this indicate that a truce agreement has been signed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this indicate that the negotiations are still ongoing?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, did anyone from the command of the 9th VPS mention an absolute cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DRLJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Drljan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rodic. Mr. Drljan, may we thank you for your attendance and the assistance that you have given to the Tribunal. You'll be pleased to know that you're now free to return to your home. Thank you very much. The usher will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we now call the next witness, if you believe that it is appropriate that we begin today and use these 20 minutes that we have left. Due to all the concerns about the time at our disposal, the Defence proposes that we use these last 20 minutes. And with your permission, we would like to call Slavoljub Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While we have a moment, could we address the scheduling over the next few days? I've been talking to Defence counsel, and we're a little bit -- our defence is a little bit behind on discovery. We should be receiving discovery for the next witness sometime this evening, and there should only be one other witness tomorrow, if that's correct. And I just want to go through the schedule so we're all on the same plate, or same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean you would like to know who is to come during the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to confirm it. We're still awaiting the proofing notes, which we'll get sometime this evening, probably between 9.30 and 11.00 tonight, which would be the final proofing notes. Which is fine. We'll deal with that tomorrow. We'll deal with that witness, as long as there's nothing significantly new. But I just want to confirm there's only one other witness after this witness tomorrow. Those are the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will depend perhaps how quick you are in cross-examination, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Even if we're quick, apparently they have no other witnesses they're bringing in tomorrow, other than one after this one. And then there appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that will depend on when this next witness finishes. When the witness finishes, there will be yet another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're under the impression, we've been told by the Defence this witness will finish, assuming cross-examination tomorrow, and there will be one other witness and that is it for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I want just some confirmation. And if there's going to be another witness tomorrow, to get some disclosure tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I see your concern. You want to know whether there will be disclosure in time for preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. So I'm under the impression it's this witness for cross-examination, assuming tomorrow, and then one other witness, and that should be it for tomorrow. And then two witnesses on Wednesday, or three witnesses on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it really just depends on how long each witness takes, and I hope you will have caught up with the growing concern of the Chamber that witnesses are taking too long in their evidence in chief and in their cross-examination. So that we certainly would not discourage witnesses being dealt with more quickly. If that means that a third witness might be reached tomorrow, so be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're under the impression, because we haven't received disclosure and I've been told by the Defence there is no third witness for tomorrow. I just want to get everything ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. Before you carry on, perhaps you'd like to sit down for just a moment. Thank you for waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I try to explain. After Mr. Stojanovic, the Defence has Mr. Kurdulija prepared as the next witness. As for the content of his evidence, we have told our learned friends about this orally. Once today's sitting is over, perhaps half an hour later, we will have prepared this in writing too, namely, what Mr. Kurdulija is going to testify about, in addition to what was disclosed under 65 ter. Your Honour, the Defence would kindly ask you for the following. Could we hear Mr. Stojanovic tomorrow? He will obviously testify in chief for a considerable amount of time tomorrow and then he will be cross-examined. And then tomorrow we hope to be able to finish both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of Mr. Kurdulija. Regrettably, as for the third witness, although he is here in The Hague, he is not yet ready to appear before the Honourable Trial Chamber. We will deal with that tonight, or whenever. I really don't know. That's the situation. I must say, though, that this situation will become even more unfavourable in view of the fact that as of tomorrow we will be working from 8.30 until 4.30. That practically leaves only the late-evening hours for proofing the witnesses. They usually finish -- start dinner at 7.00 and we get out of the courtroom at 5.00. So it is very hard for us to find time to work with them. I wish to assure you, Your Honours, that we avail ourselves of each and every moment to prepare our case, but, quite simply, there are some constraints that are objectively there and that nothing can be done about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we'll be commencing at 9.30 tomorrow, not 8.30. Be assured of that. Could the Chamber simply observe that proofing can occur during the day. There are two Defence counsel. It's not necessary for both to be in Court at the same time. So that the process of proofing can be advanced considerably using some of the sitting time as well. I think we've said enough on the subject now. If I could turn to Mr. Stojanovic. Would you mind standing, please. If you'd take the card that is being given to you and read the affirmation aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening. Could you please tell us your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Slavoljub Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am currently a professional officer, and the rank I hold is that of lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which military schools were you completed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The military academy of the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What year? When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve upon completing the military academy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The first place where I served was the reserve officers school of infantry in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of school this is in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a school that trains officers for the armed forces of the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So that was in that period of time. This is a school where there was a high level of order and discipline and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Stojanovic. The interpreters are asking you to slow down a bit so that everything could be recorded in the transcript. That is the first thing I wish to say to you. And secondly, I would like you to pause between my question and your answer so that we could indeed have everything in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What was the reputation of the school where you served, the reserve officers school in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reputation of the reserve officers school of the infantry in Bileca was a very high one. There was order and discipline and hard work. Not everybody could be a commander, and at that time, we were really appreciated both in the east and west in terms of training such officers like the infantry officers trained in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, until the 21st of September, I served in Bileca. In that period, that is to say, before the 21st of September, I handed over my duty, because I was waiting for orders from the General Staff to see where I would be sent then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In order to move on faster, could you please just give accurate answers to my questions. At some point in time, in 1991, did you receive orders for a temporary assignment to work in a unit?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the level of command that made this order regarding your assignment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you were assigned to temporarily?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was temporarily assigned to the 472nd Motorised Brigade in Trebinje, which was within the 9th Military Naval Sector and the sector was within the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you report to when you arrived in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I reported to Colonel Obrad Vicic, commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Vicic send you to any one of the units that was within the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which unit did he send you to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Motorised Company of the 3rd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive official orders at any point in time in terms of your appointment to this duty?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you received this official order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the end of February or beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which duty were you assigned to in the 3rd Motorised Company of the 3rd Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely what you said. The commander of the 3rd Motorised Company of the 3rd Motorised Brigade of the 472nd Motorised Brigade in the 9th Military Naval Sector within the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us: Where was the company deployed at the moment when you received the order, the oral order of the commander that you were being appointed leader of that company, commander of that company?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the broader area of Ivanjica. This is a village and the administrative border between the then Republic of Croatia and then Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this was an administrative border at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to point out a mistake in the transcript. Page 84, line 23, it says the 3rd Motorised Brigade of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Obviously it is the 3rd Motorised Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Do you know why you were sent to the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us why.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent in order to bring this unit up to the required level, that is to say, to bring work, order, and discipline to an appropriate level because it was not appropriate before that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question because it overlapped the answer.

utterances.speaker: SLAVOLJUB STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One of the key problems for the brigade and for the unit that I commanded was the fact that the unit was not appropriately manned with the necessary VES, military specialties. Because it was mostly reserve personnel from the area of Dubrovnik that manned this unit. Because the men of Dubrovnik did not respond to call-up, then the other regions could not provide the needed VES specialties.
